steps.body: A fraction doesn't need a pizza. The stretch of number line from **0 to 1** is a whole too — a bar lying flat. Cut that trip into equal JUMPS and every landing spot earns a fraction name. Same old rule from chapter 1: equal jumps, or no names.
Cut the trip finer and finer.

widget.prompt: The 0→1 trip starts in 2 big jumps. Slide the jump count until the trip is cut into SIXTHS.
widget.lowFeedback: The jumps are still too big — sixths need a finer cut.
widget.highFeedback: Too fine! You've cut past sixths — ease back.
widget.successFeedback: Six equal jumps: each one covers 1/6 of the trip. The line cuts just like the bar did.

predict.prompt: Right now the trip is 2 big jumps. When you cut it into SIXTHS, will each jump be longer or shorter than a half-jump?
predict.reveal: Six jumps must share the very same trip that two jumps shared — so each sixth is a much shorter stride than a half.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents nl partition.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for nl partition must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines nl partition.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: The whole trip is 1; five equal jumps split it fairly, so each jump covers 1/5 of it.
It's the fair-cut rule on its side: 5 equal pieces of the 0→1 stretch, each piece 1/5.

widget.prompt: A 0→1 number line is cut into 5 equal jumps. How much of the trip is ONE jump?

options.feedback: Five fair jumps share the trip — each carries a fifth of it.
1 is the WHOLE trip, all five jumps together. A single jump is just a fifth of that.
5 counts the jumps — it's the cut count, living downstairs in 1/5. One jump covers 1/5.
Careful — fourths would come from a 4-jump cut. This trip has five jumps, so fifth-sized pieces.

steps.body: Now the sneaky part: **marks versus jumps**. To cut the trip into 4 jumps, you draw only 3 new marks INSIDE — 0 and 1 are already standing there. Marks inside = jumps − 1. It's chapter 1's cuts-vs-pieces, wearing number-line clothes.

explanationVariants: Six jumps need five inside marks — the ends (0 and 1) are already drawn, and marks inside = jumps − 1.
Walk it: each new mark ends one jump and starts the next, so 5 marks slice the trip into 6.

widget.prompt: You want to cut the 0→1 trip into 6 equal jumps. How many NEW marks do you draw between 0 and 1?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 counts the JUMPS. The marks sit between them — and 0 and 1 already close the ends. Inside marks = jumps − 1.
7 counted the ends too — but 0 and 1 were already on the line before you picked up the pencil. Only the INSIDE marks are new: 5.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Every new mark splits one jump into two — start from 1 jump and count the marks it takes to reach 6.

widget.prompt: Tap the ONE line that is fairly cut into thirds.

hotspots.label: Line A: two inside marks, evenly spaced
Line B: two inside marks, bunched to the left
hotspots.feedback: Two marks make three jumps — but these jumps don't match. Unequal jumps earn no names, on lines as on pizzas.

hotspots.label: Line C: three inside marks, evenly spaced
hotspots.feedback: Beautifully even — but three inside marks make FOUR jumps: fourths, not thirds.

widget.missFeedback: Thirds needs exactly 3 jumps (2 inside marks) AND all jumps equal.
widget.successFeedback: Line A: two evenly spaced marks, three matching jumps — honest thirds.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents nl partition.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for nl partition must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines nl partition.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: A landing spot's name is a distance promise — 1/5 must always mean exactly one-fifth of the way. Equal jumps keep the promise.
If jumps varied, two people could stand at 'one third' in different places. Equal jumps make the name mean one exact spot.

widget.prompt: Why must the jumps on the line be EQUAL?

options.label: So each landing spot's name tells its true distance from 0
options.feedback: The name is a promise about distance — equal jumps are what make the promise real.

options.label: To make the drawing neater and easier to look at
options.feedback: Neatness is a bonus. The real reason: 'one third of the way' must mean the same exact spot for everyone.

options.label: They don't need to be — close counts as good enough
options.feedback: Close-enough breaks the map: 2/3 could land in different places on different drawings. Equal jumps pin every name to one spot.

options.label: Because unequal jumps are impossible to ever draw
options.feedback: Easy to draw, actually — line B proved it. They're just not allowed to hand out fraction names.

hints: The mile splits into 4 quarter-mile jumps.
Flags land at the END of each jump: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, and…
The lake (at 1) gets a flag; the trailhead (at 0) doesn't.
explanationVariants: Flags stand at 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, and 4/4 (the lake) — one per jump-end: 4 flags.
Four jumps, and each jump ends at a flag. The trailhead starts a jump but ends none, so it stays bare.

widget.prompt: A trail runs from the trailhead (0) to the lake (1 mile). A flag is planted at every fourth of a mile — including at the lake, but NOT at the trailhead. How many flags?

commonErrors.feedback: 3 counts only the INSIDE marks — but the lake at 4/4 gets a flag too. One flag per jump-end makes 4.
5 planted one at the trailhead — the puzzle says 0 stays bare. Count jump-ENDS only: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: List the flag spots by name: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4 — then count them.

steps.body: The line is yours to cut.
takeaways: The 0→1 stretch is a whole; equal jumps are its fair pieces.
Inside marks = jumps − 1 — the fencepost trick.
Equal jumps pin each fraction name to one exact spot.
steps.teaser: next: landing on 1/b — and busting the 'fourth mark' trap.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Lay a chocolate bar along the line from 0 to 1 — cutting the bar and cutting the trip are the SAME move. Equal pieces of bar = equal jumps of line, and each jump is one piece of the trip.

explanationVariants: Three equal jumps share the whole trip — each covers 1/3 of it.
It's a 3-piece fair cut of the 0→1 bar: each piece is a third.

widget.prompt: The 0→1 trip is cut into 3 equal jumps. One jump covers…

options.label: 1/3 of the trip
options.feedback: Three fair jumps, each a third of the way.

options.label: 3 trips
options.feedback: 3 is the jump COUNT. A single jump is one of those three: 1/3 of the trip.

options.label: 1/2 of the trip
options.feedback: Halves would be a 2-jump cut. Three jumps make thirds.
